Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Rohan, a 44-year-old single South Asian man, entered therapy with a quiet intensity, his hands clasped tightly. For years, he’d been a dedicated chef, finding solace in the precision of the kitchen, but lately, even that sanctuary felt besieged. His journey to America had been a harrowing one, fleeing conflict in his homeland over two decades ago. He vividly recalled the chaos: the desperate dash for safety, the sudden explosions, the sight of people gravely injured, the helplessness he felt as he watched events unfold, unable to intervene. He had witnessed unimaginable violence, the faces of suffering etched into his mind, and the memory of the military presence, their uniforms and weapons, still made his stomach clench.

In the years that followed, Rohan found it incredibly difficult to articulate the full horror of what he’d endured. Sometimes, he could recall fragments of what happened, but it felt as if it had occurred to a stranger, a detached, emotionless recall that left him numb. Other times, the memories would flood back with an overwhelming wave of grief, a raw, unyielding sorrow for all that was lost. These shifts in memory quality deeply fed into his conviction that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and a pervasive survival guilt gnawed at him, the belief that he had permanently changed for the worse. He was certain that the trauma had fundamentally broken something within him, a belief that solidified his negative appraisals of himself and the world. This pervasive self-blame and conviction of being irreparably damaged made him acutely sensitive to any reminders of vulnerability or past failures, turning seemingly innocuous details into potent triggers for his alarm system.

These deeply held negative appraisals, particularly his profound inaction guilt and the sense that he was permanently damaged, made him feel constantly on edge, like danger was always lurking just beneath the surface, significantly increasing his overall sense of threat. This heightened perception of threat made him acutely sensitive, turning everyday sounds and sights into potent triggers. For instance, the distant wail of an ambulance would instantly plunge him into a state of hypervigilance, his body tensing, his mind racing, making it incredibly difficult to concentrate on the complex demands of his kitchen duties. When a colleague recently started discussing a minor car accident, the casual talk about injuries immediately triggered a similar, intense threat response. His hyper-alertness meant he was always identifying escape routes whenever he entered a new space, a necessity born from the profound sense of vulnerability he carried. This constant state of alarm and hyper-alertness also made it difficult for him to calmly access and process his traumatic memories, often leaving them feeling fragmented and out of reach, or conversely, overwhelming in their intensity.

In response to these pervasive feelings of threat, Rohan had developed a repertoire of maladaptive strategies. The sound of an ambulance, or any emergency context, immediately propelled him into action, leading him to actively avoid open spaces where he felt exposed and vulnerable, preferring the enclosed, predictable environment of his kitchen. He also meticulously avoided any public spaces where he might encounter military or police uniforms, crossing streets or taking detours to prevent such encounters. When he did feel cornered or threatened, he often defaulted to a fawn response, becoming overly compliant and agreeable, hoping to de-escalate any perceived danger. These avoidance behaviours, by narrowing his world and increasing his hyper-focus on potential dangers, ironically made him even more susceptible to new triggers, as his brain was constantly scanning for cues that might justify his avoidance. These maladaptive strategies, while offering a fleeting sense of control, inadvertently maintained his heightened sense of threat, as they prevented him from ever truly testing his safety beliefs.

The self-reinforcing cycle continued to tighten its grip. His constant hypervigilance and the difficulty concentrating, born from his pervasive sense of threat, made him even more sensitive to potential triggers, turning even benign events into alarms. His avoidance of uniforms and open spaces, while providing temporary relief, paradoxically reinforced his conviction that the world was a dangerous place and that he was still in peril, further solidifying his negative appraisals. These appraisals, in turn, continued to drive his maladaptive strategies; his belief that he was permanently damaged and deserved his suffering made him less likely to challenge his avoidance, keeping him trapped. The more he relied on these strategies, such as avoiding discussions about accidents or withdrawing, the less opportunity he had to process his traumatic memories, which remained fragmented and difficult to integrate.

The cumulative effect on Rohan’s life had become undeniable. His difficulty concentrating impacted his ability to manage his kitchen staff effectively, leading to errors and increased stress. He found himself increasingly isolated, declining social invitations that involved unfamiliar or open venues. He came to therapy feeling exhausted, trapped in a cycle he couldn’t break. He was tired of the constant hypervigilance, the endless escape route planning, and the persistent guilt that shadowed his every step. What frightened him most was the thought that his belief about being permanently changed for the worse was true, and that he would never again feel truly safe or at peace. He sought help with a quiet desperation, hoping, against his own deep-seated convictions, that some part of him could still be mended.
